newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila spells out conditions before IMF exit.
newsitem.headline: Manila spells out conditions before IMF exit.

text.p: The Philippines must clear three hurdles by mid-1997 if it hopes to break free of International Monetary Fund (IMF) supervision, Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson said on Sunday.

He said these included completion of the comprehensive tax reform programme launched by President Fidel Ramos and payment by the government of its financial obligations to the country's three petroleum firms.
The Philippines also needs to fully implement an automatic oil price formula it began introducing last August, Singson said.

"We need these structural reforms in place in time to give flesh and substance to our goal of charting our own economic course and financial independence and, more important, ensure their sustainability," he said in a statement.

Under the IMF's programme for the Philippines, the country is required to meet certain targets, including keeping inflation down and restricting growth of money supply. Manila has in the past found some of the targets restrictive and wants greater control of its economic options.
Singson said the three issues had to be resolved by mid-year "if the Philippines is to graduate permanently from the IMF after 35 years and 23 programmes under IMF conditional lending".
The Philippines enacted in November a new tax law on beer and cigarettes but bills restructuring corporate and individual income taxes are still pending in Congress.

The government also has to pay oil companies 2.4 billion pesos ($92 million) in dues from the Oil Price Stablisation Fund (OPSF), a buffer fund meant to help soften the impact of fluctuations in international crude prices. The oil firms' claims on the fund had grown larger as world prices rose.
Officials have said they expect the automatic oil pricing formula, adopted in advance of the planned full deregulation of the oil industry, to be fully implemented by April.

The formula allowed monthly adjustments in pump prices of petroleum products based on movements in Singapore posted prices. Previously, pump prices were adjusted on the basis of the landed cost of crude and the foreign exchange rate.
Singson said in an interview published in the Sunday Chronicle that an IMF mission would visit Manila in February to review its programme with the Philippines.
"We hope to be able to make an exit (in mid-1977)," the newspaper quoted him as saying.
Singson said the Philippines was projecting an inflation rate of six to seven percent this year from the average annual inflation for 1996 of about 8.5 percent.

"We are also expecting in 1997 a higher economic growth, meaning a higher GNP (gross national product). We are projecting a range of 7 percent to eight percent, a stable peso just like in 1996 and a somewhat lower interest rate," he said in the interview.
Economists said GNP for 1996 would likely hit an eight-year high of 7.1 percent.
